title: Japanese Jazz Fusion
description: The sound of Japanese fusion in the 70s and 80s, then the artists who defined it and what sets each one apart.

segments.title: The sound of Japanese fusion
segments.summary: What fusion is, how Japan made its own version, and how to recognize it.
segments.narration:
Welcome. This lesson is about Japanese jazz fusion, the music Japan made in the late seventies and the eighties. First we will talk about the style itself. Then we will meet the main artists one by one, and listen for what makes each of them different.

Fusion started in the United States around nineteen seventy. Musicians like Miles Davis, Weather Report and Return to Forever took jazz harmony and improvisation and plugged them into rock and funk: electric guitars, electric bass, synthesizers, loud drums. Japanese musicians loved that music, and Japan already had a big, serious jazz audience. So by the late seventies, Japan had its own fusion scene.

But it did not sound like the American version. Here is what to listen for.

One: melody comes first. American fusion could be dark, long and very improvised. Japanese fusion is built around catchy themes, almost like pop songs without a singer. You can hum most of these tunes.

Two: it is bright. Lots of major keys, sunny chords, an optimistic mood. Fans often call it the sound of summer, of driving by the sea.

Three: precision. The arrangements are tight, the bands play complex lines perfectly together, and the production is very clean. Solos are there, but they are shorter and planned to fit the song.

Four: it is close to city pop, the Japanese pop of the same years. Many of these musicians also played on pop records, so the two styles share the same sound.

The first track is California Shower by saxophonist Sadao Watanabe, from nineteen seventy eight. He recorded it in Los Angeles with American musicians like Dave Grusin and Lee Ritenour, and it became one of his best known records. It is the easy, sunny side of the style. Then comes Raisins, by guitarist Ryo Kawasaki, who moved to New York and played with American jazz greats. It is funkier and closer to the American sound. Compare the two.

segments.title: Masayoshi Takanaka, the guitar that sings
segments.summary: Takanaka's tropical, melodic guitar and his showman spirit.
segments.narration:
Our first artist is guitarist Masayoshi Takanaka. Before going solo, he played in the Sadistic Mika Band, a Japanese rock group, and you can hear that rock background in his sound.

What sets Takanaka apart is that his guitar sings. He plays the melody the way a vocalist would: long notes that bend and cry, simple phrases you remember after one listen. Other fusion guitarists want to impress you with speed. Takanaka wants you to sing along.

The second thing is the mood. His music is tropical. You will hear Latin and samba rhythms, percussion, steel drums, the feeling of a beach holiday. Even the album covers are full of sun and sea. If Japanese fusion is the sound of summer, Takanaka is the one who made that the most obvious.

The third thing is fun. He is a showman, famous for playing a guitar built inside a real surfboard. His music is not trying to be serious art. It is trying to make you feel good, and it does.

So, when you listen, ask yourself: could a singer perform this melody? With Takanaka, the answer is almost always yes.

First you will hear Blue Lagoon, his most famous track. Listen to the opening theme, and then to how the solo stays melodic instead of racing. Then comes Ready to Fly. Notice the Latin groove under the guitar.

segments.title: Casiopea, the precision band
segments.summary: Casiopea's tight ensemble playing, slap bass and complex unison lines.
segments.narration:
Next is Casiopea, the band that many fans see as the heart of Japanese fusion. It was formed in nineteen seventy six by guitarist Issei Noro, who also wrote most of the songs.

Takanaka is about one voice. Casiopea is about the whole band. Four musicians playing as one machine. Their trademark is the unison line: a fast, complicated melody that guitar, keyboard and bass play together, note for note, perfectly in time. It sounds simple and happy, but try to follow it and you will realize how hard it is.

Listen also to the bass. Tetsuo Sakurai plays slap bass, hitting and popping the strings with his thumb and fingers. That gives Casiopea its punchy, funky bounce. Under him, drummer Akira Jimbo plays very busy, detailed patterns, but always clean.

On top of that, keyboardist Minoru Mukaiya adds bright synthesizer sounds that place this music right in the early eighties.

So what makes Casiopea different? Takanaka is relaxed and tropical. Casiopea is energetic and technical, almost athletic, but they never lose the pop melody.

You will hear two songs from Mint Jams, from nineteen eighty two, which many fans see as their essential record. First Asayake, which means morning glow. Listen to the guitar theme, then wait for the bass. Then Domino Line, where the whole band locks into one long chain of notes, falling like dominoes.

segments.title: T-Square, melody you can't forget
segments.summary: T-Square's anthem-like themes, the wind synthesizer, and their place in TV and games.
segments.narration:
Casiopea's great rival was T-Square, a band that started in nineteen seventy eight as The Square. The two bands are often compared, so let's be clear about the difference.

Casiopea leads with the guitar and the rhythm section. T-Square leads with a wind instrument. For years their front man was Takeshi Itoh, on saxophone and on the EWI, the electronic wind instrument. It looks like a clarinet, but it plays synthesizer sounds. That gives T-Square its signature tone: a smooth, almost vocal lead that can soar over the band.

The second difference is the writing. Guitarist Masahiro Andoh wrote many of their songs, and his themes are anthems: big, emotional melodies that build and lift, made to be played in stadiums and on television. Where Casiopea impresses you, T-Square tries to move you.

That is why their music spread so far beyond jazz fans. Their song Truth, from nineteen eighty seven, became the theme of Formula One broadcasts on Japanese television, and generations of Japanese viewers know it. Andoh also composed music for the video game Gran Turismo, so even if you never heard of T-Square, you may have heard their sound.

First comes Truth. Listen for the wind synthesizer taking the melody, and how the song builds like a race start. Then Omens of Love, a gentler song written by keyboardist Hirotaka Izumi, and one of the most played pieces by Japanese school brass bands.

segments.title: Kazumi Watanabe, the virtuoso
segments.summary: Kazumi Watanabe's harder, rock-jazz guitar, and how the four artists compare.
segments.narration:
Last artist: guitarist Kazumi Watanabe. He is the one who breaks the rules we described at the start.

Watanabe is the virtuoso of the scene. His playing is fast, sharp and full of difficult jazz ideas, with a rock edge. Where Takanaka sings and T-Square goes for big emotional themes, Watanabe likes tension: strange chords, odd turns, solos that push hard. He is the closest of the four to the American fusion we talked about in the first lesson.

He was also very connected to the wider music world. He toured with Yellow Magic Orchestra, the famous Japanese electronic band, and in nineteen eighty he released To Chi Ka, one of his best known albums.

So here is the whole map, one more time. Sadao Watanabe and Ryo Kawasaki showed two doors into the style: sunny and easy, or funky and close to New York. Takanaka is the singing, tropical guitar. Casiopea is the precise, energetic band. T-Square is the big melody and the wind synthesizer. And Kazumi Watanabe is the virtuoso who keeps one foot in serious jazz.

The last track is Unicorn, from To Chi Ka. Listen to how the theme is still catchy, but the solo gets wild. If you liked this lesson, a good next step is city pop, the sister style of everything you heard today. Thanks for listening.
